Ward
WORD
noun
From the Old English weard, “a watching, a guard,” kin to warden and to the German Wart; hence the act of watching, the place of watching, the body of men who watch, the custody in which one is held, and the charge appointed to a man.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ward is the old word for watch and custody together — the guarding, the guard, the guard-post, and the place where the guarded are kept. Scripture uses every sense. It is a prison: Pharaoh put the butler and the baker into the house of the captain of the guard, “and they continued a season in ward” (Gen 40:4), and it was there, in Joseph’s long custody, that God set the hinge of Israel’s deliverance. It is the guard-post of a jail: when the angel led Peter out, “they were past the first and the second ward” before the iron gate opened to them of his own accord (Act 12:10) — two watches and a bolted gate could not hold a man God meant to walk free. It is an appointed course of service: David’s singers cast lots “ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar” (1Ch 25:8), each house taking its turn in the courses of praise. And it is a charge in the house of God: Nehemiah cleansed the people from all strangers “and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business” (Neh 13:30). So the word gathers a doctrine of ordered watchfulness. God’s house is not a crowd but a roster; every man has his ward and stands in it. The saint is himself kept in ward — not by Pharaoh but by power divine, kept through faith unto salvation. Joseph in ward and Peter past the wards preach the same LORD: the custody of men cannot hold, and the custody of God cannot fail.

Webster 1828 Definition

The act of watching or guarding; a garrison or guard-post; custody or confinement; an appointed charge or course of duty.

expand to see more

WARD, the act of guarding; watch; the state of being guarded.

A place of confinement; custody; a prison, as Joseph in ward (Gen 40:4).

A guard-post or station of watchmen, as the first and second ward (Act 12:10).

An appointed course or turn of service, ward against ward (1Ch 25:8).

A charge committed to a man in the house of God (Neh 13:30).

Key Scripture

Gen 40:4 — "And the captain of the guard charged Joseph with them, and he served them: and they continued a season in ward."

Act 12:10 — "When they were past the first and the second ward, they came unto the iron gate that leadeth unto the city; which opened to them of his own accord: and they went out, and passed on through one street; and forthwith the angel departed from him."

1Ch 25:8 — "And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar."

Neh 13:30 — "Thus cleansed I them from all strangers, and appointed the wards of the priests and the Levites, every one in his business;"

Modern Corruption

An old word for watch, custody, and appointed charge; it recovers ordered service in God’s house and the keeping of His own.

expand to see more

The word rebukes an age that will keep no watch and take no post. In David’s house the singers cast lots ward against ward, small and great, teacher and scholar alike, that none should be idle and none should be lord; Nehemiah appointed the wards of the priests and Levites, every one in his business. God’s house is a roster, not a mob: every member has a ward, and to stand in it faithfully when no eye sees is the whole of the duty. The modern temper wants the church without the charge — the singing without the courses, the membership without the watch. But a ward unmanned is a gate unguarded, and the flock is spoiled where the watchman sleeps.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the double custody of God. Joseph continued a season in ward, forgotten by the butler he had served, and every day of that prison was laying the foundation of a nation’s bread. Peter slept between two soldiers and walked past the first and the second ward, and the iron gate opened of his own accord. The custody of men is never final; the LORD keeps the keys of Pharaoh’s prison and Herod’s. And the saint himself is held in a better ward — kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, a custody no gate can open and no enemy can storm.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the act of watching, the place or body that watches, the custody held, and the charge appointed.

expand to see more

Ward — Old English weard, “a watching, a guard.”

Kin to warden and warder; the one who keeps the watch.

It denotes custody: Joseph continued a season in ward (Gen 40:4).

It denotes a guard-post: the first and the second ward (Act 12:10).

It denotes an appointed charge: ward against ward (1Ch 25:8).

Usage

"Joseph continued a season in ward, and God was building Egypt’s granaries all the while."

"Peter passed the first and the second ward: no watch holds the man heaven means to free."

"They cast lots ward against ward — in God’s house every man has his post and keeps it."
